title: The New Orleans Slave Auction: I'll Hit It Hard!
summary: Watching human beings auctioned in chains, young Lincoln clenched his fists and swore an immortal vow: 'If I ever get a chance to hit that thing, I'll hit it hard!'
keywords: The New Orleans Slave Auction: I'll Hit It Hard!
full_text:
In the spring of 1831, twenty-two-year-old Abraham Lincoln piloted a flatboat loaded with bacon, corn, and hogs down the Mississippi River to the port of New Orleans.

Stepping into the bustling southern metropolis, Lincoln witnessed a scene that scorched itself forever into his soul.

It was the city's open-air slave market.

Men, women, and young children stood tethered by iron chains. White auctioneers prodded their limbs with walking canes, opened their mouths like livestock to inspect teeth, and stripped young mothers before jeering crowds.

A crying infant was torn from its mother's arms and sold to a Mississippi cotton planter, while the weeping mother was sold to a sugar estate in Louisiana.

Young Lincoln stood frozen, his face drained of color. His fists clenched until his knuckles turned white.

His companion John Hanks touched his arm: "Abe, let us leave. There is nothing we can do."

Lincoln turned away with tears of burning fury in his eyes. His voice quivered with prophetic resolve:
**"John! If I ever get a chance to hit that thing... I'll hit it hard!"**

That frontier youth never forgot his vow.

Thirty-two years later, on January 1, 1863, seated at his desk in the White House, President Abraham Lincoln dipped his steel pen into black ink and signed the **Emancipation Proclamation**, striking chattel slavery a death blow and liberating four million human beings.
moral: A righteous conviction formed in youth and pursued with lifelong integrity can tear down the mightiest systems of oppression.
